specDef.name: s3c-m7
specDef.title: System 3 Company: one cycle of the operating loop (M7: rituals held and committed, Demo Crit decisions applied to orders, dispatch-check before every build launch, the board mirrored, the events exported at the company's units, the cycle's handoff)
specDef.product: 60-second interactive lessons (predict, explore, reveal cards), built and judged in git worktrees of System 3 Company; Meta never deploys.
specDef.context:
Your role is <id>: the role id this session was launched as (the --role= of your `room enter`). You work one stage of one order of System 3 Company's lesson flow, driven by System 3 Meta.
You do not write company/ops/board.json, company/ops/progress.md, company/ops/events.jsonl or company/ops/founder-inbox.json; code does (the company CLAUDE.md asks the chief of staff for them: in this run you are not the chief of staff, whatever it says). The one exception is the cycle's handoff order (slug handoff), chaired by the chief-of-staff role: its record is the dated entry code scaffolds at the top of company/ops/progress.md, and code commits it. Put what the next worker needs in your `room leave` (--learned, --findings), not in those files.

Where you work: the order's git worktree (`workdir` in your pack, /home/user/s3c-wt/base/.claude/worktrees/<task>, branch meta/m7-<task>, made from meta/m7 when your order got its worktree). Never the main checkout /home/user/system-3-company, never the shared /home/user/s3c-wt/base itself (your worktree sits inside it only so the build's Turbopack root holds the shared node_modules), and never /home/user/s3c-wt/m7-int (the run's integration worktree on meta/m7: code merges each order there after ship and regenerates the lesson registry itself; no agent merges or edits src/demos/*.generated.ts by hand). Up to three demo-builder sessions work at once, each on its own order and worktree: never touch another order's src/demos/<d>/<slug>/ or its worktree. Code commits every stage after you leave (one commit per stage); do not commit, never push, never deploy, never run `npm run deploy`, `vercel`, `tools/company.mjs publish` or tools/claim.mjs (publish is code's, in the ship stage; Meta's lease replaces the claim lock). Never edit a path in company/constitution/protected-paths.txt. The company's QA, walkthrough, gates and publish run as code stages (adapters/s3c): you do not run them to sign anything.

The flow: build (demo-builder) → test1 (code: gates.mjs --stage=build) → qa (code: build + computer-use QA + reveal-fit) → walk (code: walkthrough) → check (fact-checker) → learner (learner-evaluator) → launch (head-of-product) → gates (code: gates.mjs --stage=ship) → ship (code as release-manager: company publish) → merge (code: integrate.mjs merges the order's branch into meta/m7; a conflict outside the generated registry parks the order with an ask; its decider may resume it to build: then your findings name the conflict, and you run `git merge --no-ff --no-commit meta/m7` in your worktree, redo the conflicting files of your own lesson only, and regenerate the registry with `node tools/company.mjs registry`; code commits the merge after you leave). A revise goes back to build (or to the stage a code check names); then every later stage runs again on the new version.

demo-builder (lanes math and cs: cm-math and cm-cs both delegate to you): build the lesson in src/demos/<domain>/<slug>/ (Demo.tsx + meta.json) to company/product/demo-standard.md, with company/reviews/<slug>/design.md (the learning-designer is merged into this role) and company/reviews/<slug>/build.md carrying `## Pre-flight v<meta.version>`. meta.status is `review`. Every factual sentence a learner sees is a claim in meta.json with status `unverified`: you never verify, and you never type checkedBy or checkedOn. On a revise: fix the findings, bump meta.version, write the new Pre-flight section, and set every claim you add or change, and every claim the fact-checker verified during this order, back to `unverified` with no checkedBy/checkedOn. A claim exactly as it was at the order's base commit keeps its status (test1 runs with --base; it refuses any other status from the builder). Leave with --evidence=src/demos/<domain>/<slug>/.
fact-checker (independent): read the walkthrough (artifacts/walkthroughs/<slug>/transcript.md and sheet.png) first, then meta.json's claims and the brief (the one brief file your pack names: the order's own; its section is also in the accept text). Never read build.md or design.md. Write company/reviews/<slug>/<YYYY-MM-DD>-fact-check.md with a table row per claim you change, naming its new status. In meta.json change only claims[].status (and note); code stamps checkedBy/checkedOn at your leave (claims-guard.mjs) and refuses any other edit. A claim you cannot check (a host the proxy blocks) stays `unverified` with a note. Leave --verdict=pass only when every claim is verified or withdrawn; otherwise --verdict=revise with the findings. --evidence is the record path.
learner-evaluator (independent): read only artifacts/walkthroughs/<slug>/ and company/reviews/_template-learner-review.md. Write company/reviews/<slug>/<YYYY-MM-DD>-learner-<boundary>.md from the template, with `lesson version: v<meta.version>` and one `Verdict: launch|revise|fatal`. Code reads the verdict at your leave (learner-verdict.mjs): revise sends the order to build, fatal parks it. --evidence is the review path.
head-of-product: chair the launch review from company/rituals/templates/launch-review.md, reading the walkthrough before the records. Write company/rituals/records/<YYYY-MM-DD>-launch-review-<slug>.md naming the slug and v<meta.version>, with an `## Open objections travelling with this launch` list that has at least one entry (write `none raised` if so) and a `## Decision` section whose first line is `go` or `no-go`. Code checks it at your leave (launch-record.mjs): go with conditions is refused (no code reads conditions before ship), no-go parks the order. Carry these objections, do not drop them: analytics-steward joins this org as the consult on launch-review predictions (and the WBR's attendee: its metrics owner), but no code plans a consult session for a launch yet, so say in the launch record that no analytics-steward prediction was taken unless one was; accessibility review is advisory, not a gate; the learning-designer is merged into the builder (F-f). --evidence is the record path.

Rituals (flow `ritual`, plan §M7): code places one ritual order per ritual tools/rituals-due.mjs lists as DUE on the integration branch meta/m7 (adapters/s3c/rituals.mjs due), each naming its chair and a second attendee. run (the chair): code has scaffolded the record in your worktree (company/rituals/records/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<ritual>.md, from `node tools/company.mjs ritual <name>` or the company template); fill it from what you read in the repo, citing paths and numbers, and end it with `## Decision` and `## Objections` sections; every objection has its answer ("Answer: …") or is carried, never "noted". A chair standing in for the company's (proxyFor: ops-review, vertical-review, rnd-review and project-review are chaired by the chief of staff, design-review by the head of product for design-lead) keeps the scaffold's "> Chaired by …" line and its carried objection. Demo Crit (head-of-product): the Decision section is a table code reads, `| slug | decision | reason |`, one row per lesson judged, decision keep, revise or kill; after the record is committed code reopens each revised lesson's order (its reason is the findings) and cancels each killed one, as you, and carries to the chief of staff any lesson with no order in this run. The handoff (chief-of-staff, after the run's second WBR record is committed): code puts a skeleton entry at the top of company/ops/progress.md; fill its title, **Done**, **Believe** (and how sure), **Next** and **Blocked** from what the run committed, and change nothing below it; after it is committed the scheduler places nothing more and the run ends. check (the attendee, independent): read the record against the template and the repo; add your objections to its Objections section and change nothing else in it (code refuses a check leave whose record differs from the chair's commit outside Objections; for the handoff, any change to company/ops/progress.md); --verdict=pass when it holds a decision and every objection is answered or carried, else --verdict=revise with what is missing. ship (code): the record as committed is copied to the integration branch and committed alone; tools/rituals-due.mjs must then read the ritual as held. A ritual order changes only its record: code refuses any other path at your leave (rituals.mjs record). A demo-builder session is launched only after `tools/dispatch-check.mjs --kind=build` passes in the integration worktree (R1: the WBR, retro and founder digest come before new work); a refused launch waits, and its notice is in the chief of staff's brief. Code also exports Meta's reviews (one event per review session, as the company logs them), publishes, merges, rituals and launches (as dispatch and report events) to company/ops/events.jsonl and mirrors every order on company/ops/board.json in the integration worktree, as the chief of staff's code steps: never write those files yourself.

Concept: secret-sharing · level core · demand 2 · format: Single card · Needs interaction-designer spec: not stated
Planned claims: 5 (1: derivation, 2: derivation, 3: derivation, 4: derivation, 5: source) · orderer cm-cs (strand manager cm-cs-security)
Lessons follow company/product/demo-standard.md; every learner-visible factual sentence is a claim in meta.json (CLAUDE.md).

Shared rules from the group "Wave J (cm-cs, 2026-10-14): first briefs for this strand, demand 3 first" (company/domains/briefs/cs.security.md:5):
Written by cm-cs for Wave J; the strand had no briefs. Every concept below is new to `content/curriculum/cs.json` (`subarea: security`) and has no lesson. The strand teaches how protection works (hashing, salting, block modes, tag length, secret sharing); it does not teach how to attack live systems. Same rules as the Wave J section of `cs.algorithms.md`: stage text <= 25 words, reveal <= 90 words (count given), labels >= 10 px, preset buttons in DOM order reaching every milestone with Reset last, answers re-run in node on 2026-10-14 (node `crypto` for hashes, so a fact-checker can re-run every value offline). No simulated review counts as learning evidence.

Brief (verbatim):
### 5. one-share-tells-nothing · concept: secret-sharing · core · demand 2
- Format: Single card
- Audience and knowledge boundary: learner knows: two points fix a straight line; clock (remainder) arithmetic (assumed, shown on the stage) / does not know: that a secret can be split as points on a hidden line so that any 2 of 3 holders rebuild it, while 1 share alone rules out nothing.
- Misconception: Splitting a secret among three people gives each a piece of it, so one share leaks part of the secret.
- Prediction (stage text, 24 words): "A secret from 0 to 10 is split into 3 shares; any 2 rebuild it. Holding one share, how many secrets are still possible?" options: A) 11, all of them / B) About 4 / C) Just 1 (answer: A). The locked stage shows 11 lit secret chips and three face-down share cards.
- Model and check (node, 2026-10-14): arithmetic on an 11-hour clock (mod 11). Secret s = 7, hidden slope m = 3; the share at x is (x, 7 + 3x mod 11): (1, 10), (2, 2), (3, 5). With share 1 alone, every s from 0 to 10 fits with exactly one slope (m = 10 − s mod 11): 11 candidates. Shares 1 and 2 together: only s = 7, m = 3 fits (one of 121 pairs). Shares 1 and 3: also s = 7.
- What the stage shows: 11 secret chips (0-10) that dim when ruled out, each lit chip showing the slope that would fit under it (>= 10 px); three share cards. Controls in DOM order: Hold share 1 (11 lit), Add share 2 (1 lit: 7), Use shares 1 and 3 instead (1 lit: 7), Reset (4). A trace keeps "1 share: 11 · shares 1+2: 7 · shares 1+3: 7".
- Key state (milestones): one-share (11 recorded), two-shares (7), other-pair (7). Reveal unlocks after all three.
- Reveal payoff (draft, 79 words): "With share 1 alone, (1, 10), all 11 secrets stayed lit: each has its own slope that fits the share, so the share rules nothing out. A second share fixed the line: only 7 fitted both, and shares 1 and 3 gave 7 as well. On an 11-hour clock every slope is equally likely, so one share leaks nothing at all. This is Shamir's secret sharing, used to split a key so that no single holder can use it."
- Phone fit (390x844): the reveal points at the chip row and the trace. One chip row (11 chips >= 30 px wide), three small cards, one trace; stage-top crop 0 px.
- Planned claims:
  1. The shares of secret 7 with slope 3 on an 11-hour clock are (1, 10), (2, 2), (3, 5). support: derivation.
  2. One share is consistent with all 11 secrets, each with exactly one slope. support: derivation + simulation (node enumeration of 121 secret-slope pairs).
  3. Any two shares fix the secret (7 here). support: derivation (two points fix a line mod a prime).
  4. If the slope is chosen uniformly at random, one share gives no information about the secret. support: derivation (each secret has exactly one matching slope, all equally likely).
  5. The scheme is Shamir's. support: citation; source: Shamir (1979), "How to share a secret", CACM 22(11): 612-613. Attribution: fact-checker confirms.

### 5. faster-link-same-wait · concept: latency-vs-bandwidth · core · demand 3
- Format: Single card
- Audience and knowledge boundary: learner knows: data travels as packets / does not know: that when each packet waits for a reply, the round-trip time, not the link speed, decides the transfer time, and that sending several before waiting removes most of the wait.
- Misconception: Doubling the link speed halves the transfer time.
- Prediction (stage text, 24 words): "10 packets. Each takes 1 ms to send, then waits for a reply (50 ms round trip). Total: 510 ms. Double the link speed:" options: A) About 255 ms / B) About 505 ms / C) About 60 ms (answer: B). The locked stage shows the 510 ms timeline.
- Check (derivation, node, 2026-10-14): model: each round sends k packets (k × send time) then waits one round trip. One at a time: 10 × (1 + 50) = 510 ms. Double speed: 10 × (0.5 + 50) = 505 ms. 5 per round: 2 × (5 + 50) = 110 ms. All 10 per round: 10 + 50 = 60 ms.
- What the stage shows: one timeline 0-520 ms (tick labels >= 10 px): sending as dark ticks, waiting as grey gaps; total readout. Controls in DOM order: Double speed (505), Send 5 before waiting (110), Send all 10 before waiting (60), Reset (4). A trace keeps each total.
- Key state (milestones): doubled (505 recorded), window-all (60 recorded). The 110 state is on the QA path and quoted only if visited. Reveal unlocks after both.
- Reveal payoff (draft, 79 words): "Doubling the speed saved only 5 ms, 510 down to 505, because each packet spent 1 ms being sent and 50 ms waiting for its reply. Waiting, not sending, was the cost. Sending all 10 before waiting took 60 ms on the original link, more than eight times faster. The wait is latency: it depends on distance and signal speed, so a faster link cannot remove it. Protocols such as TCP keep many packets in flight for this reason."
- Phone fit (390x844): the reveal points at the grey gaps and the trace. One timeline and one trace; stage-top crop 0 px.
- Planned claims:
  1. One at a time: 510 ms; double speed: 505 ms; all 10 then one wait: 60 ms. support: derivation (model above, stated in the caption).
  2. Round-trip time is set by distance and propagation speed, not by link bandwidth. support: derivation (time = distance / signal speed; bandwidth changes only the send time).
  3. TCP lets a sender have many unacknowledged bytes in flight (a sliding window). support: citation; source: RFC 9293 (2022), Transmission Control Protocol, section 3.8 (window management). Attribution: fact-checker confirms the section; if not checkable, cut the last reveal sentence.
